summary: ModVoteEscrow is a 192-line veCRV-style lock: users lock an ERC20 for 1 week to 4 years, hold a weight of amount x timeLeft / maxLock that decays linearly, and cannot transfer it. Per-user math (balanceOf, lock creation/extension/top-up, withdrawal after expiry) is correct and withdraw() follows checks-effects-interactions; rounding drift between bias/slope and the sum of balances is a few wei; there are no owner powers to abuse; and flash-locking is economically meaningless because a lock buys weight in proportion to its duration (a 1-week lock is 1/208 of a 4-year one). The worst thing found is a global-accounting bug rather than a per-user one: checkpoint() records lastPoint as the raw block.timestamp, so the week-by-week walk in checkpoint() and totalSupply() never lands on the week-aligned slopeChanges keys and expired locks' slope is never removed. Confirmed with forge on the compiled contract, totalSupply() falls to exactly 0 while a 4-year locker still holds ~249 ve, and the corruption is permanent. Since the block's whole purpose in the catalog is to be the quorum denominator for ModGovernor and the boost denominator for ModGauge, that is a governance/emissions integrity failure (quorum decays to zero; boosts are wrong in both directions). Two medium issues follow: quorum is a live ratio with no snapshot and no execution deadline, and fee-on-transfer tokens strand the last withdrawers. It is NOT safe to wire this block into a governor or gauge as-is; as a standalone time-lock over a plain ERC20 with nobody reading totalSupply, it holds funds correctly.

findings.title: checkpoint() walks from an unaligned lastPoint, so expired locks' slope is never removed: totalSupply undercounts and decays to zero while locks are still live
findings.where: checkpoint() L86-L100 (lastPoint = block.timestamp at L99), totalSupply() L65-L82, _addWeight() L106, createLock() L125
findings.detail: Lock ends are floored to week boundaries (L125, L152) and each lock's slope is scheduled for removal at `slopeChanges[end]` (L106) with a week-aligned key. The constructor aligns `lastPoint` (L53), but checkpoint() then stores `lastPoint = block.timestamp` (L99), an arbitrary second. From the very first lock onward both checkpoint() and totalSupply() step `next = t + WEEK` from that unaligned point, so `next` is never a multiple of WEEK and `slopeChanges[next]` (L77, L93) always reads 0. Curve avoids this by re-aligning `t_i = (last_checkpoint / WEEK) * WEEK` at the start of every walk; this contract does not. The consequence is that the global `slope` only ever grows (or is reduced by _removeWeight for locks that are re-locked while still active), while `bias` keeps decaying at the slope of locks that have already expired and been withdrawn. Confirmed with forge on the compiled contract: two 1,000-token locks (4 weeks and 4 years); at week 8 totalSupply()=938.4 vs sum(balanceOf)=958.2; at week 52 516.4 vs 747.3; at week 156 totalSupply()=0 while the 4-year locker still holds 248.6 ve, and the stored `slope` is exactly 2x that user's slope. The error is permanent and unrepairable: nothing ever decrements the orphaned slope, there is no admin reset, and every new lock's bias is then decayed at the inflated rate. Note the storage path is the one that matters: totalSupply() at L65 starts from the corrupted stored `slope`, so calling checkpoint() more often does not help. Composition impact: ModGovernor.quorum() = votes.totalSupply() * quorumBps / 1e4 (governor.sol L106-L107) falls below the configured share of real weight and eventually to 0, at which point state() (L116) only needs forVotes > againstVotes; ModGauge.workingBalanceFor() (gauge.sol L85-L88) divides by escrow.totalSupply(), so every ve holder's share is overstated (max 2.5x boost for a sliver of ve, diluting un-boosted stakers) and once veTotal hits 0 the `veTotal == 0 -> base` branch strips boost from everyone who actually locked.
findings.exploit: 1. Deploy ModVoteEscrow(token, 4y) and ModGovernor(votes = escrow, quorumBps = 2000), wire the governor as owner of a ModVault / mintable ModToken. 2. Honest users lock; some choose short locks (weeks). 3. Every short lock that expires leaves its slope in `slope` forever (slopeChanges[end] is never read). After enough expiries -- in the test, one 4-week lock equal in size to the 4-year lock is enough by week 156 -- totalSupply() returns 0 while long lockers still hold real weight. 4. Attacker locks a trivial amount for one week (weight = amount * 7d / 4y), calls propose(...) (proposalThreshold defaults to 0), waits votingDelay, castVote(id, true). 5. quorum() == 0, so at end of votingPeriod state(id) == Succeeded as long as nobody voted against; attacker calls execute(id) and the governor-owned block does whatever the calldata says (setOwner, mint, setStrategy). Even before totalSupply reaches 0, quorum is silently lower than configured. Gauge variant: stake with a dust ve lock and receive the full 2.5x boost because balanceOf/veTotal is inflated.
findings.recommendation: Re-align the walk every time: in checkpoint() and totalSupply() start from `t = (lastPoint / WEEK) * WEEK`, and for each step decay by `slope * (min(next, block.timestamp) - lastT)` where lastT starts at the real lastPoint (not a full WEEK on the first partial step), then apply `slopeChanges[next]` and continue. Alternatively store `lastPoint` week-aligned and keep a separate `lastTs` for the partial tail. Add an invariant test that sum(balanceOf) == totalSupply() (+/- rounding) across expiries. Keep the 208-week cap but document that anyone should call checkpoint() at least once per ~4 years or scheduled changes beyond the cap are skipped. Until fixed, do not wire this block into ModGovernor as `votes` or into ModGauge as `escrow`.

findings.title: Live, unsnapshotted totalSupply turns governor quorum into a moving target: defeated proposals become executable as weight decays, and a late lock can block a passed one
findings.where: totalSupply() L65-L82 and balanceOf() L58-L62; consumers governor.sol quorum() L106-L107, state() L116, execute() L173-L177
findings.detail: The escrow exposes only current-time weights; there is no getPastVotes / getPastTotalSupply. ModGovernor evaluates state() lazily and quorum() live, and a Succeeded proposal has no execution deadline. Because ve totalSupply decays monotonically between lock actions (by design, and far faster with VEESCROW-1), a proposal that failed quorum at the end of voting flips from Defeated to Succeeded simply by waiting until quorum() falls below its frozen forVotes, and anyone can then execute it. The opposite direction also exists: a large holder can createLock/increaseUnlockTime after voting ends (front-running execute) to push quorum above forVotes and flip a passed proposal to Defeated. The vote weights themselves are non-transferable, so the flash-vote and transfer-and-revote games the token block suffers from are genuinely closed here; the residual issue is the supply side of the quorum ratio.
findings.exploit: 1. Governor: quorumBps = 2000, escrow totalSupply = 1,000,000 ve at vote end, so quorum = 200,000. Attacker's proposal gathers 150,000 for / 0 against -> Defeated. 2. Nobody cancels it (only guardian or proposer can; proposer is the attacker). 3. Weight decays; when totalSupply() <= 750,000 (weeks to months, or immediately once VEESCROW-1 has pushed supply to zero), state(id) == Succeeded. 4. Attacker calls execute(id). Blocking variant: proposal passes with 210,000 for; whale locks 100,000 tokens for 4 years in the same block as execute() -> quorum rises to ~220,000 -> execute reverts NOT_EXECUTABLE.
findings.recommendation: Have the governor snapshot quorum at proposal creation (store `quorumAt = votes.totalSupply() * quorumBps / 1e4` in propose, or use a start-of-vote checkpoint) and add an execution window after which Succeeded expires. If the escrow is to serve a snapshotting governor, add per-user and global point history (Curve's user_point_history / point_history with balanceOfAt / totalSupplyAt). Deployers using the blocks as-is should set the guardian to an active multisig that cancels stale proposals.

findings.title: Lock amount is recorded as requested, not received: fee-on-transfer or deflationary tokens leave the last withdrawers unable to exit
findings.where: createLock() L129-L131, increaseAmount() L142-L144, withdraw() L170-L171
findings.detail: `token.pull(msg.sender, amount)` is followed by `locks[msg.sender].amount = amount` and `totalLocked += amount` without measuring the escrow's balance delta. The `token` input is a free `erc20` port, so a deployer can wire any token. With a fee-on-transfer or negatively rebasing token the contract holds less than totalLocked; withdraw() pushes the full recorded amount, so early withdrawers are paid in full and the last ones revert on PUSH_FAILED with no way out. Weights are also computed on the phantom amount, so voting/boost power is overstated relative to what is actually escrowed. There is no owner rescue or sweep, so the shortfall is permanent.
findings.exploit: 1. Deploy the escrow over a token that charges 1% on transfer. 2. Alice locks 100 (escrow receives 99, records 100); Bob locks 100 (escrow holds 198, totalLocked 200). 3. Both locks expire. Alice withdraws 100 -> escrow holds 98. 4. Bob.withdraw() tries to push 100 -> transfer fails -> revert; Bob's 99 tokens are stuck forever.
findings.recommendation: Measure `received = balanceAfter - balanceBefore` around pull() and use that for the lock amount, weight and totalLocked; or explicitly document that only plain ERC20s (no fees, no rebasing, no hooks) are supported and have the composer refuse to wire known fee-on-transfer tokens. Consider a permissionless `sweep(token != locked)` for stray tokens.

findings.title: Token pull happens before lock state is written: a sender-hook token can re-enter increaseAmount()/createLock() and permanently inflate totalSupply
findings.detail: Both functions call `token.pull()` (external call) before updating `locks[msg.sender]`, `totalLocked` and the global weight. No reentrancy guard exists. With a token that calls the sender during transferFrom (ERC777 tokensToSend, or any hook token), the sender can re-enter increaseAmount(): the inner call runs _removeWeight on the still-old `l.amount` (L141 again, absorbed by the `bias > weight ? .. : 0` clamp at L113), pulls, adds weight for a+x; the outer call then adds weight for a+2x. Net result confirmed with forge: after one re-entry a lock of 3,000 tokens has balanceOf = 2,991 ve but totalSupply() = 4,983 ve and the global slope is overstated to match. Nothing corrects it later. The attacker keeps all their tokens (withdrawable at expiry), so the cost is only lock time. Effects: governor quorum inflated (denial of governance), gauge boosts of everyone else diluted. withdraw() is correctly checks-effects-interactions (state zeroed at L168-L170 before push at L171), so there is no fund-drain path; plain ERC20s such as the catalog's ModToken have no hooks, which is why this is low rather than medium.
findings.exploit: 1. Escrow deployed over a token with a sender-side transfer hook. 2. Attacker contract locks a (createLock). 3. Calls increaseAmount(x); in the tokensToSend hook it calls increaseAmount(x) again. 4. Both pulls succeed (attacker paid 2x, lock records a+2x - correct for the user), but bias/slope were credited W(a+x)+W(a+2x) against only one effective removal, so totalSupply() exceeds the sum of balances by up to W(a+x) for the life of the lock. 5. Repeat to push quorum arbitrarily high or to dilute gauge boosts.
findings.recommendation: Move `token.pull()` after all state writes in createLock() and increaseAmount() (the checkpoint/_removeWeight/_addWeight/lock write can all precede the pull), and/or add a simple nonReentrant modifier on createLock, increaseAmount, increaseUnlockTime and withdraw.

findings.title: The owner / governor port has no powers and there is no emergency exit -- which is correct for a vote-escrow, but deployers should know the wire is inert
findings.where: contract ModVoteEscrow is Owned L14, constructor L44-L54; Owned common.sol L33-L51
findings.detail: Owned is inherited and the catalog offers a `governor` input for the owner slot, but no function in the contract is onlyOwner. The owner cannot pause, change maxLock (immutable), rescue tokens, or shorten anyone's lock. This is the desirable property for a vote-escrow (no rug, no owner-side quorum games) and it means the catalog docs' promise holds on this axis. The flip side is that locked funds are unrecoverable until `end` no matter what -- including if the locked token is upgraded/migrated, or if VEESCROW-1/3 make the deployment unusable -- and stray tokens sent to the contract are stuck.
findings.exploit: Not exploitable. Operational scenario: a deployer wires ModGovernor into the `governor` port expecting governance to be able to pause or migrate the escrow; a bug is found; there is nothing to call. Users with 4-year locks wait 4 years.
findings.recommendation: Either drop the Owned inheritance and the `governor` input from the catalog entry so the composer does not imply control, or add a narrowly scoped, timelocked `enableEarlyUnlock()` (one-way, all users, forfeits weight) for migration. Say in the block docs that locks are irrevocable and the owner is a no-op.

findings.title: The `erc20` port is read-only: transfers revert and decimals is a constant 18 regardless of the locked token
findings.where: decimals L22, balanceOf() L58-L62, transfer()/transferFrom()/approve() L177-L187
findings.detail: The block advertises `provides: [escrow, erc20]`. Reverting transfer paths are the point (non-transferable votes), but on the canvas the same port can be dragged into any erc20 slot -- vault asset, AMM token, gauge stakeToken/rewardToken, treasury payout token -- and every one of those will revert on pull/push at first use. No funds are lost (the revert happens before anything moves), the block is just dead. Separately, `decimals` returns 18 while balanceOf is denominated in the underlying token's raw units (amount * timeLeft / maxLock). Over a 6-decimal token a ve balance of 1e6 is one whole ve, not 1e-12; a deployer setting ModGovernor.proposalThreshold or reading dashboards in 18-decimal terms will be off by 1e12.
findings.exploit: Not a security exploit. Misconfiguration path: escrow over USDC-like 6-decimal token; governor proposalThreshold set to 1000e18 expecting '1000 ve' -> nobody can ever propose, since max possible weight is totalLocked in 6-decimal units.
findings.recommendation: Return `IERC20(token).decimals()` (read once in the constructor into an immutable) instead of a constant. In the catalog, mark the erc20 output as `erc20:nontransferable` (or only expose the `escrow` port) so the composer refuses to wire it into transfer-consuming inputs.

safe_use: Do not wire this block as ModGovernor `votes` or ModGauge `escrow` until VEESCROW-1 is fixed (re-align the checkpoint walk to week boundaries); totalSupply() is wrong from the first expired lock onward and can never be repaired on a live deployment.
Lock only plain ERC20s: no fee-on-transfer, no rebasing, no transfer hooks. The catalog ModToken qualifies; arbitrary external tokens may not (VEESCROW-3, VEESCROW-4).

If used with a governor anyway, set quorumBps conservatively, set proposalThreshold above dust, keep an active guardian that cancels stale proposals, and add an execution deadline -- a Defeated proposal becomes Succeeded as weight decays (VEESCROW-2).
Tell users the lock is irrevocable: no owner, no pause, no early exit, maxLock is immutable. The `governor` input in the catalog wires an owner that can do nothing (VEESCROW-5).

Do not drag the escrow's `erc20` output into any slot that moves tokens (vault asset, AMM, gauge stake/reward, treasury) -- every transfer reverts. Read balances in the underlying token's decimals, not 18 (VEESCROW-6).

Minimum effective lock is the next week boundary (can be seconds away) and weight scales with duration, so a short lock is cheap but weightless; do not treat a non-zero balanceOf as meaningful without a duration check in the consumer.
Anyone can call checkpoint(); after the fix, ensure it is called at least once every 4 years (208 weeks) or scheduled slope changes beyond the walk cap are skipped.
